This is game 106 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (153,689 bytes)
- count.py (828 bytes)
- libs.py (1,378 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

I'm checking the liberties around F4, J4, H3 and worried the group could get into trouble if I don't block the open end near J5. I'm now considering whether I can form two eyes using the corner points around H1, J1, J2, J3, H3, J4, focusing on whether H3 needs to be secured.

I'm tracing out Black's threats — the F3 chain, the G2 atari sequence into G1/H1 connections — to see if playing G1 first is sente and helps build eye shape in the J1/J2/H3/J3 area, versus just solidifying with H3 now to connect my whole group and check its liberties.

Trying J3 instead: surrounding H3 with G3, H2, H4, J3 makes it a real eye as long as J2/J4 aren't black, since only G2 counts as an enemy diagonal. Then I need a second eye around J1/J2 with H1 support, checking whether J2's neighbors stay safe.

I'm tracing out how black's hane at G1 and push at J4/J5 would reduce liberties on J3 and whether I can still hold both eyes by playing H1 in response, keeping H1's neighbors clear.

Trying a different move order: play J3 first, and if black hanes at G1, I just connect at H1, which should secure two eyes — one at H3 surrounded entirely by my own stones, and another at J1/J2 whose neighbors are also all mine.

Checking the group connectivity: even if I split into chains like G3-G4-H4, H1-H2, and J3, they all touch the same two eye points, H3 and J2/J1, so black can't fill either eye and the shape lives.

But wait — if the G3-G4-H4 chain only touches H3 as its internal liberty and not J2, black could first fill the outside liberties F4/J4, reducing it to one liberty at H3, then play H3 itself to capture it since all of H3's neighbors would be white. That's the classic false-eye scenario — the chains aren't actually connected through a shared point, so the eye isn't guaranteed real.

Checking the diagonals around H3 (G2 black, G4 white, J2 eye, J4 uncertain): if J4 turns black too, two diagonals are bad and H3 becomes false. So I need to secure J4, or otherwise connect the groups, to make this eye genuine. Maybe playing J4 now and letting stones at G3, G4, H4, J4, H2 form the shape, then responding to black's G1 push with H1, turns the interior points H3-J3-J2-J1 into a bent four shape in the corner that should live.

This is getting too tangled — if black plays J2, J1 stops being a clean eye since its neighbor is black, so that response causes problems. I'm trying a cleaner alternative where H3 connects solidly into the main chain, giving liberties at F4 and J4 to work with instead.

I'm tracing through the capturing races around J2/J3/H3, checking which black placements die versus leave a surviving eye shape, trying to confirm whether this corner group stays dead after each forcing sequence.

I lost game 106 as White against the 12k: I resigned at move 38 after my bottom-right invasion group died.

1. Count the liberties of the invading group.
2. Take any first-line point that Black could place on and connect out.
3. Only then block the open end.
